analysis:
The only changes are in MiMoV26NativeLoadTransaction.swift. Head adds a private optional hook property `mediaReservationRemovalHookForTesting` at line 299. `removeSettledMediaReservation` (head ~1096-1109) now removes the entry under the lock, returns the hook, and invokes it outside the lock. A new internal setter, `setMediaReservationRemovalHookForTesting`, assigns the hook under the lock.

Security behavior is unchanged. Removal still requires `reservation.isFullyRetired` and an identity match (`===`) before the dictionary entry is dropped. The hook is called after the lock is released, so there is no lock-order inversion or reentrancy under the transaction lock. Retirement checks at base 1321 (`mediaReservations.isEmpty` gating `permitSettlement`) are unaffected, because removal remains atomic with the identity check. The hook takes no data and receives no request content, keys or paths, so it is not a disclosure channel.

The setter is non-private, so any in-module code could install a callback. Visibility is the same as the existing `setUsageReaderPreparationHookForTesting`. The hook is observation only and cannot alter ownership, retire a reservation or grant memory credit. It is not reachable from the coordinator wire boundary or from consumers. A hostile-provider adversary who controls the process already holds TB-003 capabilities, so this adds no meaningful attack surface.

A minor behavior change: the hook runs only when the entry was actually removed, which is stricter than before. No finding was identified against T-041, the A-018 availability threats or the TB-007 inference-engine boundary. I verified only the supplied excerpts and did not review unchanged callers of `removeSettledMediaReservation`.
